existing_graph_source_evidence.title: Ranajit Guha, Elementary Aspects of Peasant Insurgency in Colonial India (1983; Duke edition 1999).

verification.note: Duke description and contents checked for insurgent consciousness, dominance/subordination, deliberate peasant political action and the original 1983 versus 1999 edition. James C. Scott wrote the later foreword. No full primary book read; a search-result PDF proved to be Banerjee’s different 2020 book and was excluded. The intervention does not certify homogeneous peasant consciousness or a single path to nationalism. Addendum 2026-10-14: Primary text now read for the Guha person entry. Introduction pp. 1–17 OCR'd at 300 dpi from a scan of the Duke University Press 1999 printing (foreword by James C. Scott) hosted by Berhampore Girls' College; preface dated Canberra, January 1983; the text keeps the 1983 Oxford pagination, checked against the Digital Library of India scan of the Delhi 1983 edition (Internet Archive dli.bengal.10689.12632; imprint 'First published 1983, Second impression 1986'). Quoted: 'Insurgency was thus the necessary antithesis of colonialism' (p. 2); 'a discourse of power'; the peasant 'denied recognition as a subject of history' (p. 3); 'a consciousness'; spontaneity 'elitist as well as erroneous' (p. 4); Gramsci on spontaneity; Hobsbawm's 'pioneering work' and 'pre-political' (p. 5); 'helps little in understanding the experience of colonial India'; 'nothing ... that was not political' (p. 6); 'a composite apparatus of dominance' (p. 8); 'negative and inversive procedure' (p. 9); limits that define 'the quality of that politics' (p. 10); 'inchoate and naive' (p. 11); Gramsci's 'pillars of politics' and 'elementary aspects' (p. 12); 'its sovereignty, its consistency and its logic' (p. 13); reading rebel consciousness in counter-insurgency records (pp. 14–15). Bibliography: Gramsci, Selections (1971); Hobsbawm, Primitive Rebels (Manchester, 1959); Hobsbawm and Rudé, Captain Swing (1969). Pp. 89–90 (Thompson on the Blacks; Hobsbawm's 'social banditry') read in the 1983 edition's text. Scott's foreword: Elementary Aspects 'became, in effect, the founding document' of 'the Subaltern Studies School' (p. ix). The rest of the book is unread.

existing_graph_source_evidence.title: Antoine Meillet, “Comment les mots changent de sens,” L’Année sociologique 9 (1904–1905), published 1906, 6–43.

verification.note: Primary section I opening and selected discussion of social groups, occupational vocabularies, borrowing and semantic change read. Meillet explicitly applies Durkheim’s externality/coercion definition to language. This documents Meillet’s reception, not direct Durkheim influence on Saussure. His introductory equation of languages with nations is a historical assumption, not adopted as a general description of multilingual societies. Individual etymologies not independently checked.

existing_graph_source_evidence.title: E. P. Thompson, “Time, Work-Discipline, and Industrial Capitalism,” Past & Present 38 (1967): 56–97.

verification.note: Downloaded primary scan: opening pp. 56–62 and selected concluding passages pp. 89–97 read; some extracted passages/notes were truncated, so no full-article reading claimed. Explicit resources include Le Goff, Febvre, Evans-Pritchard and Bourdieu. Employment relations complicate task/clock distinctions; education, religion and coercion matter alongside clocks. Concluding criticism of Moore/Kerr/Siegel contests treating workers as inert inputs. Thompson’s own developmental assumptions and cultural comparisons remain situated arguments, not a proven universal sequence.

existing_graph_source_evidence.title: Natalie Zemon Davis, Women on the Margins: Three Seventeenth-Century Lives (1995), consulted third printing/first paperback (1997), selected primary passages.

verification.note: Public OCR read: title/edition; complete prologue pp. 1–4, conclusion pp. 203–216 and acknowledgments pp. 340–344; selected Glikl opening pp. 6–8 and conclusion notes 1–8/start of 9. This primary selection supplements, rather than retroactively upgrades, the existing catalogue record.

existing_graph_source_evidence.title: Natalie Zemon Davis, A Life of Learning: Charles Homer Haskins Lecture for 1997, ACLS Occasional Paper 39 (New York: American Council of Learned Societies, 1997).

verification.note: Read for revision 1.143 (data/extension-2026/davis-backfill-2026-10-17/evidence-davis.md §1): read in full in the ACLS PDF text layer. Printed folios 10–23 appear in the text; folios 1–9 were fixed from the constant PDF offset (PDF page = printed page + 6), checked against 10–23. The unsigned ACLS preface is unpaginated and is a separate reader statement. Passages used: Bloch, Strange Defeat (p. 5) and Feudal Society (p. 7); Marx and Weber tested on Lyon (p. 7); history of the book (p. 10); multiple social axes (p. 11); ‘A Trade Union’ (1966) and Hobsbawm (pp. 12–13); Annales histoire totale ‘could not serve as a model’ (p. 13); Van Gennep, Bakhtin, and reading Evans-Pritchard, Turner, Geertz and Mintz ‘eclectically’ (p. 14); Society and Culture and ‘Rites’ (p. 15); the 1971 course with Jill Conway, ‘the first course in women’s history in Canada’ (p. 16); film and ‘anthropological history’ (pp. 17–18); ‘I came to microhistory (or what I called ethnography) via film’ and co-teaching with Geertz (p. 19); Fiction in the Archives and Stone (p. 21); ‘a decentered comparison of three European lives’ (p. 21); margins and colonial intrusion (p. 22); ‘permanently relocated as an historian of Europe’ (p. 23). Retrospective testimony (1997): evidence of how she later described her work, not of what the earlier works say.

independent_count_recomputation: Read the frozen dissertations table and retain in_analysis=True. Join citations to authorship for exact person keys and deduplicate dissertation IDs across all authorship positions; separately join works.first_author_key for first-author totals. Work leads count exact work_id citations. Dated counts require a nonempty integer dissertation year. All thirteen screened author-key all-authorship totals and every displayed work total matched the release values; first-author totals were independently computed rather than inferred from those totals.
